title: Prayer ones the soul (ch. 43)
hook: prayer unites the soul to God
tomorrow: how do you write a whole book without picking up a pen?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a servant in a ditch, hurt while running to serve, and a lord whose look held no blame. The line was he fell rushing to serve.

Inside a kitchen cabinet door, a list in a grandmother's handwriting. Names. A surgery. A job. Somebody far from home. Some lines have a check mark beside them. Some don't, and she still reads every one aloud each morning. Her granddaughter asks her once: if half of them never happened, why keep going? She doesn't answer right away. Julian of Norwich has an answer, and it begins with who started the asking.
screen: `A LIST INSIDE A CABINET DOOR.` → `SOME CHECKED, SOME NOT.` → `WHY KEEP GOING?`

segments.voice: First, the start. In chapter forty-one, Julian hears our Lord say that he is the ground of our asking. First it's his will that we have something; then he makes us want it; then he makes us ask. So prayer doesn't begin with us talking God into anything. It begins with him. Second, the dry days. She is told to pray inwardly even when it seems to have no taste at all, because that prayer is still welcome to him. Third, the line that names today. In chapter forty-three she says prayer ones the soul to God. Ones is her old word for makes one. Her reasoning: the soul is always like God in its nature, but often unlike him in its condition, through sin. Prayer makes it like him again, wanting what he wants. Fourth, back to the cabinet. On Julian's reading, that list isn't a vending machine with a broken slot. Saying those names every morning does its main work whether the check marks come or not: it keeps the one praying close to God, of one will with him. Catholics don't stop asking for things; in the Gospels Jesus tells his followers to ask. But for Julian, asking is a road, and the place it leads is oneness.
screen: `HE IS THE GROUND OF OUR ASKING.` · `PRAY EVEN WHEN IT'S DRY.` · `PRAYER ONES THE SOUL TO GOD.` · `NOT A VENDING MACHINE.` · then, large: `PRAYER ONES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let one thing you've been asking for come to mind. Hold it out without pushing, and let your attention move from the answer to the one you're asking. For those who pray, the asking can become the prayer itself: to want what God wants.
Prayer ones the soul. Julian's line: prayer makes the soul one with God, of one will with him.
Hold onto this: prayer ones, even on the days the answer is no. Go gently.

notes: Chapter 41 paraphrased: 'I am Ground of thy beseeching: first it is my will that thou have it; and after, I make thee to will it; and after, I make thee to beseech it'; and 'pray inwardly, though thee thinketh it savour thee not', for such prayer is profitable and welcome. Confirm wording and chapter.

Chapter 43 paraphrased: 'Prayer oneth the soul to God'; though the soul is ever like to God in kind and substance, restored by grace, it is oft unlike in condition by sin on man's part; prayer is a witness that the soul wills as God wills, and makes it like to God. Confirm. Kept as paraphrase; a Keeper may choose to quote Warrack exactly.
'Ones is her old word for makes one' is a gloss of Julian's 'oneth', not an etymology claim.
Matthew 7:7 paraphrased ('Jesus tells his followers to ask').
The hook's grandmother and her list are an illustrative scene, not a source.
